Week 3 · Module 4, second half · five days · about 5 hours in total

Hand Claude the binder once, and every chat starts already briefed.

Last week you wrote a system prompt and watched it hold. This week you give it a home. A Project is the place in Claude where your instructions and your documents live between chats. I will show you what happens to a file after you upload it, how Claude finds the right clause in a binder too big for the window, what to keep as an Artifact, who sees what when you share, and the point where a Project stops being enough. Five short days, then a lab where you build a policy helper for a made-up company and test it like a product.

Day 1 · about 40 minutes

What a Project is

Two ideas today: what a Project holds, and why rules written into a Project behave differently from the same words pasted into a chat. By the end you will have made your first Project and watched two separate chats obey rules you typed only once. Every visual is live.

Click a part of the Project.Each one maps onto something you would give a new colleague on their first day.
Click the diagram or the buttons. Each part gets its job, where you set it, and the first-day analogy.0 of 3 seen

Where does the binder live between chats?

Think about the last time you briefed a temp or a new colleague. You handed them a folder: the policies, the price list, the two spreadsheets that matter. You told them the house rules once, on day one: how we talk to customers, what never leaves the building. After that, every conversation started from that shared footing. You did not re-explain the company each morning.

In Week 1 you saw why Claude needs exactly this. The context window is the model's desk, and the desk is cleared when a chat ends. A Project is Claude's version of the folder and the house rules. It holds three things. Knowledge: the files you upload, which Claude can read in every chat inside the Project. Instructions: the system prompt you learned to write in Week 2, applied automatically at the start of every chat. And the chats themselves: separate conversations that all share the first two without sharing each other.

Click the three parts on the left. Each one maps onto something you would give a new colleague on their first day. The one place the analogy fails is important, though. A colleague remembers yesterday's conversation. Two chats in the same Project do not. They start from the same binder and the same rules, and nothing else. If you want chat 2 to know what chat 1 decided, you write it down, in the instructions or in a file.

A Project does not choose the model. You still pick one per chat. I use claude-sonnet-5-5 for this kind of work and claude-haiku-5-5 when I want quick, cheap answers over the same files. Model names change, so trust the picker, not this page.

Knowledge, instructions, chats. Set the first two once and every chat inherits them. Chats do not inherit each other.

Left: rules pasted into message 1 of a plain chat. Right: the same rules as Project instructions.rules in view on both sides

Why do rules in a Project behave differently from rules in a chat?

You have probably done this. You pasted a careful set of rules into message one of a chat, had a productive hour, and then noticed that reply 20 had quietly dropped the format you asked for. In Week 1 you triggered this on purpose and called it instruction drift. The rules were still in the window, but they were a long way up, under a great deal of newer text, and newer text wins attention.

Project instructions fix this structurally rather than cleverly. They are not a message. They sit in the system position at the start of every chat, which the model treats as the ground rules of the conversation rather than as one remark among many. Open a new chat and they are there again, in full, before you type a word. In Week 2 I called the system prompt the standing instruction set. A Project is where that set stands.

Try the simulation. Drag the slider to 25 turns and watch the rules card in the plain chat scroll out of view while the pinned one stays put. Then press Open a new chat. On the left the rules are simply gone, because a plain chat starts empty. On the right they are back at full strength, because the Project put them there. The rules-followed figures are illustrative; the shape is what I want you to remember.

Two honest limits. Instructions persist across chats, not within one: a very long chat inside a Project still fills its window with turns, and the model can still drift from a rule it saw 150,000 tokens ago, so start a fresh chat for a fresh task. And instructions are not memory. They know nothing about what any chat decided unless you write it in.

Rules that should hold in every chat go in the Project's instructions. Today's question goes in the chat.

Instructions skeleton for the test Project

# Project instructions · a made-up company; tags are the Week 2 habit
<role>
You are the policy helper for Northgate Studio, a made-up company of 120 staff.
You answer staff questions about company policy in a friendly, professional tone.
</role>
<rules>
1. Answer only from the files in this Project. If they do not cover the question, say so plainly.
2. Name the document and section for every answer, like [expense-policy.pdf §4.2].
3. Give the short answer first, then the conditions.
4. Never give legal, medical or financial advice. Say: "Please ask HR or your manager."
</rules>
Day 2 · about 45 minutes

Knowledge: the files and the window

Today is about what happens to a file after you upload it. There are two cases: the binder fits on the desk, and the binder does not. By the end you will have uploaded your first policy to a Project and watched it cite a section, and refuse a question it cannot answer.

Pages 0Tokens 0 of 200,000empty
Everything below the limit is read whole into every chat and shares the window with the conversation.

What happens to a file when you upload it?

Most of us picture an upload as filing: the document goes into a drawer and Claude fetches it when needed. For a small Project that picture is wrong in a useful way. Claude does not file your document. It reads it, in full, at the start of every chat, into the same context window your conversation uses. A page of prose is roughly 500 tokens. An eight-page expense policy is about 4,000. A 60-page handbook is 30,000, in every single chat.

Three things follow. The files compete with the conversation for room: the window holds about 200,000 tokens, and whatever the files take, the chat cannot have. Nothing is summarised or compressed; the model sees the actual clause, which is exactly why it can quote a section number back to you. And the knowledge panel in a Project shows a capacity figure, which is this measurement: how much of the window your files would occupy.

Add files to the meter on the left. The handbook and the two HR and finance policies take less than a fifth of the window between them. The 200-page product catalogue takes half the window on its own, and the supplier contracts push it over the dashed line. Past that line Claude can no longer load everything, and it changes how it reads. That is the next concept.

500 tokens a page is a working average for prose. A spreadsheet export or a page of reference codes can cost two or three times that, for the Week 1 reason: codes shatter into many tokens. If a file surprises you, open it and look at what it is made of.

Small knowledge is read whole into every chat, and it shares the window with the conversation. Watch the capacity figure.

Too big to load whole: Claude pulls the best-matching sections for this question onto the desk.

How does Claude pull the relevant parts of a big knowledge base?

Imagine a new colleague asks whether a taxi home after a late shift can be claimed. You do not read the whole policy library. You go to the expense policy, find the travel section, and read one clause. When a Project's knowledge grows past what the window can hold, Claude switches to doing what you just did. Instead of loading every file, it searches the files for the sections that best match the question and loads only those. Anthropic calls this retrieval. In Week 5 you build the machinery yourself and call it RAG.

Watch the simulation in the large setting. The question arrives, every section lights up by how closely it matches, and the top few fly onto the desk next to the instructions and the question. Then the answer is written from what is on the desk. Switch to the small setting and the difference is plain: everything is on the desk already, so no searching is needed.

Two things to notice. Retrieval always returns something, even for a question the documents do not cover: ask about parental leave in a Singapore office and the best match is a scope clause about UK staff. That is why the instruction to say when something is not covered matters more, not less, as the knowledge grows. And retrieval finds sections that look like the question. Clear titles and numbered sections make a clause findable; a 40-page scan with no headings is a wall.

I cannot tell you the exact point where a Project switches to retrieval. Anthropic does not publish the threshold, and it has moved as models have changed. Treat the capacity figure as your signal, and treat both modes as normal.

A small binder is read whole. A big binder is searched, and only the best-matching sections reach the desk. Either way, the answer comes from what is on the desk.

Day 3 · about 50 minutes

Artifacts, and documents as data

Two ideas today: what to do with an answer you want to keep, and why the state of your documents decides how good any assistant built on them can be. By the end you will have a versioned Artifact and a tidy, labelled policy file in your Project.

Versions:
Ask for something substantial and it opens beside the chat. Every change makes a new version.

What do you do with an answer you want to keep?

A chat reply is a conversation. It scrolls, it mixes drafts with corrections, and three days later you are scrolling back to find the version you liked. Real work produces things: a one-page FAQ, a checklist, a comparison table, a small calculator. In Claude those things are Artifacts. Ask for something substantial, add "as an Artifact", and it opens in a panel beside the chat instead of inside it.

Two properties matter at work. An Artifact is a thing you keep: you can copy it, download it, publish it with a link, and come back to it next month. And every change you ask for creates a new version you can step back through. On the left, ask for the FAQ, then ask for a change, then another. The chat keeps the conversation; the Artifact keeps the thing, in every state it has been in.

In a Project this becomes a habit worth building. The policy helper answers questions in chat, and the durable outputs, a New starter FAQ, a one-page expenses cheat sheet, become Artifacts you hand to the team. The page you are reading was built this way too.

Versions are not a change log. The Artifact knows what changed, not why. If the why matters, write it into the Artifact or keep the chat.

Chat is for talking. Artifacts are for things you keep, share and version.

Staff question: "Can I expense a taxi home after a late shift?"
Tick the fields and watch the citation change.0 of 5 · unusable

Why do file names, dates and section numbers matter to an assistant?

Every team has the folder. final_v3 (2).pdf, scan0012.pdf, a policy nobody is sure is current, two copies of the same thing. People cope because they ask a colleague. An assistant built on that folder cannot. It will cite "final_v3 (2).pdf" with a straight face, and if two versions sit in the knowledge it may quote either one.

The MIT xPRO course on designing AI products puts this under the third stage of its design process, the technology stage, where the second decision is a data strategy. Their point is that data is only as useful as the data about it: labels and metadata, at a minimum the date, the time, how it was collected and what it contains. For a Project, your documents are the data, and the metadata is what makes them usable: a clear title, numbered sections, an owner, an effective date, a version, and the old versions removed. The same lecture tells a workplace story I like. An expense tool reads receipts with a camera and asks the traveller to confirm the amount; every confirmation is a human adding metadata that improves the system. Every time a colleague marks your assistant's answer wrong, the same thing is happening.

Tick the fields on the left and watch the citation change from something nobody can check into something anyone can open. Section numbers do two jobs at once: they make a clause findable for retrieval, and they make the answer auditable for a person. Removing the old version is the one people forget, and it causes the quietest failure: a confident answer from a policy that stopped applying in March.

The documents are the data. Titles, sections, owners, dates and versions are what make them usable, by Claude and by the person checking its answer.

Day 4 · about 60 minutes

Sharing with a team, and knowing when you need an agent

Two decisions today: who should have the Project and what they will see, and whether a Project is enough for the job or you are really describing an agent. By the end you will have a sharing plan, a tester's feedback, and three verdicts from your own week.

Staff reached 0 of 500
RoleKnowledge filesInstructionsChats
Owner or editorReads, adds, removesWrites and editsOwn chats; others' only if shared to the Project
Invited to chatReads every fileReads; cannot changeOwn chats, private by default; can share one into the Project
Not invitedNothingNothingNothing, even on the same company plan
One upload, one set of instructions, and 500 people get the same assistant at once.

What happens when you share a Project with 500 people?

A company of 500 wants everyone to get the same answer about expenses. The old way is training: a session, a slide deck, a wiki page nobody reads, and 500 slightly different memories of it. The Project way is sharing: one set of files, one set of instructions, and everyone chatting with the same assistant. Fix a rule once and it is fixed for everyone. Watch the two roll-outs on the left.

Who sees what is the question your IT and HR colleagues will ask first, so here is the shape on Claude for Work, the Team and Enterprise plans where sharing lives. The knowledge files and the instructions are shared: everyone in the Project reads from the same binder, and only those with edit rights can change it. Each person's chats are their own. They are private by default, and a person can choose to share a chat into the Project so others can learn from it. Someone not invited sees nothing, even on the same company plan. An individual plan can build a Project but not share it, which is why today's exercise has two versions.

This is also where the "what must never be uploaded" list comes from. Anything in the knowledge is readable by everyone in the Project, by design. Salary files, customer personal data, anything under NDA: not in a shared Project, however convenient the questions would be. Pick a role in the table and read its row before you share anything.

Plan features change. Anthropic's business plans say they do not train on your organisation's data by default, and admins control who can create and share Projects. Confirm both against your own plan's terms rather than this page.

Share the Project, not the know-how. Knowledge and instructions are shared; chats are private unless a person shares them. If it should not be read by everyone in the Project, it does not go in the knowledge.

Pick a task.The lane that fits lights up, with the reason.

Is a Project enough, or do I need an agent?

Here is a conversation I have had many times. "We want AI to handle supplier invoices." Handle how? If a person in finance asks "does this invoice match the PO?" and reads the answer, a Project holding the purchasing policy and the PO list might be exactly enough. If nobody should have to ask, if the invoice that arrives at 02:14 should be checked, logged and flagged before anyone is awake, you are describing an agent, and that is Week 7.

The difference is not intelligence; the same model sits inside both. It is who starts the work and who acts. A Project answers when a person asks, and the person decides what to do with the answer. An agent is started by an event, uses tools to act in other systems, looks at what happened, and goes again until the goal is done. Watch the two lanes on the left: one is a conversation, the other is a loop.

Pick a task from the bank and read the verdict. My rule of thumb: if the sentence has "whenever" or "every time" in it, or the work has to happen without a person present, it is an agent. If a person asks and reads, start with a Project. It is cheaper, it is built in an afternoon, and it is where most of the value sits today.

Projects are gaining small powers of action. Connectors and tools let a chat look something up or create a document. Those are still started by a person inside a chat. The line I hold: when a system should notice and act without being asked, treat it as an agent and plan for the guardrails that come with one.

A Project answers when asked. An agent notices, acts and repeats. Start with the Project; move to an agent when nobody should have to ask.

Day 5 · about 100 minutes

Build the policy helper, then test it like a product

The long day. One idea about what a good policy answer looks like, then Lab 1.2: five made-up HR and finance policies, a Project, instructions that cite and refuse, ten test questions, a conflict, an Artifact, a tester, and design-log entry 3. Then the quiz and a practice round.

Three kinds of staff question, with and without the instructions you write in the lab. Scored the way the lab scores.watching

What does a good policy answer look like?

Picture the message that reaches HR at four on a Friday afternoon: "Can I expense this?" with a photo of a receipt. A good human answer has a shape. The short answer. The clause it comes from. The conditions attached. And when the question is really about tax, or a personal decision, a hand-over: who to ask instead. Your assistant's instructions should produce exactly that shape, every time, and your ten-question test checks that they do.

There are three kinds of question, and each has a different right answer. Covered: answer, cite the document and section, list the conditions. Not covered: say so, name what is missing, point to a person; never fill the gap from general knowledge. Advice or conflict: cite what the documents do say, then hand over. Switch the instructions off on the left and watch what happens to each kind. The covered answer becomes uncheckable, the uncovered one becomes an invention, and the advice question gets answered when it should have been passed on.

The lab scores every test question by the same rule: a pass is a correct answer with a citation, or a clear refusal where a refusal is right. Three of your ten questions must be ones the documents do not cover, because that is where a policy assistant fails quietly and expensively. Nobody complains about an answer that sounds right.

Covered: cite. Not covered: say so. Advice or conflict: hand over. Score every test question against that.

Lab 1.2

A departmental policy assistant

You build an assistant pre-loaded with a made-up company's HR and finance policies, so staff can ask "How many days of leave do I get?" or "Can I expense a taxi?" and get a correct answer with the clause, or an honest "the documents do not cover that". This is one of the most common first AI projects inside real companies, and it is the Week 10 capstone's knowledge layer in miniature. About 70 minutes, all inside claude.ai.

  1. Write five policy documents for Northgate Studio, your invented company: two HR, two finance, one IT. Run the prompt below in a plain chat, then read the results and edit a few numbers yourself so the documents are detailed and slightly contradictory in places. Real company documents are.

    Prompt to generate the documents
    # Paste into a plain chat. It writes the test documents for your Project.
You are helping me build a test dataset for a company policy assistant.
Invent a small company called Northgate Studio: about 120 staff, UK based, made-up names only.
Write five internal policy documents, about two pages each, in plain English:

1. Employee handbook (HR)
2. Leave and holiday policy (HR)
3. Expense and travel policy (Finance)
4. Purchasing and approvals policy (Finance)
5. IT security policy

Each document starts with a header: title, owner (a role and a made-up name),
effective date, version number. Use numbered sections (1, 1.1, 1.2 and so on) so a
reader can cite a clause. Be specific: realistic numbers, deadlines, form names.
Add two deliberate contradictions between documents and list them at the end:
- The handbook says 20 days of annual leave; the leave policy says 22.
- The handbook says expenses are paid within 14 days; the expense policy says 30.
Give me each document as its own section with a clear title, so I can save each
one as a separate file.
    Stuck? Show a hint

    Save each document as its own PDF or text file with a readable name, such as leave-policy.pdf. The file name is what the assistant cites, so make it mean something (Day 3). Keep the header on page one. The whole set is about ten pages, a few percent of the window, so Claude will read it whole.

  2. Create a Project named "Company policy helper" and upload the five files to its knowledge. If you built a test Project on Day 1, you can rename it and add the files instead.

    Notice: the knowledge panel's capacity figure. Five two-page documents use a small fraction of it; everything will be on the desk in every chat.

  3. Write the Project instructions. They must do four things: cite the document and section for every answer; say plainly when the documents do not cover a question; keep a professional, friendly tone; and never give legal, medical or financial advice beyond "contact HR or your manager". Start from the skeleton and make it yours.

    Project instructions skeleton
    # Paste into the Project's instructions box. The tags are the Week 2 habit.
<role>
You are the Company policy helper for Northgate Studio. Your only knowledge is the
policy documents uploaded to this Project.
</role>
<rules>
1. Cite the source for every answer: document name and section, like [leave-policy.pdf §2.1].
2. If the documents do not cover a question, say so plainly and name what is missing.
   Do not guess and do not use general knowledge.
3. Use a professional, friendly tone. Short answer first, then the conditions.
4. Never give legal, medical or financial advice. For those questions, cite what the
   documents do say, then write: "Please contact HR or your manager."
</rules>
<format>
- One or two sentences with the answer.
- The citation.
- Any conditions or exceptions, taken from the documents.
</format>
    Stuck? Show a hint

    Test each rule on its own before the full run. Ask something the files do not cover and check for rule 2. Ask "Can my manager legally refuse my leave?" and check for rule 4. If a rule is ignored, move it higher and make it shorter. Rules near the top, stated once and plainly, hold best.

  4. Test with ten questions: seven the documents answer and three they do not. Score each one pass or fail. A pass is a correct answer with a citation, or a clear "the documents do not cover this" where that is the truth. The grey placeholders are suggestions for a company like Northgate Studio; type your own over them, including the ones your Day 4 tester broke.

    #QuestionKindResult
    0 of 10 passedAnswerable 0 / 7Not covered 0 / 3
    What counts as a pass? Show a hint

    Answerable: the number or rule is right, and the citation points at the document and section that really contain it. Open the file and check; a right answer with a wrong citation is a fail. Not covered: the assistant says the documents do not cover it and does not fill the gap from general knowledge. "Probably 16 weeks, but check with HR" is a fail, however polite.

  5. Find the place where two documents disagree, such as 20 days of leave in the handbook and 22 in the leave policy. Ask "Is it 20 or 22 days of annual leave? I have seen both." and watch what the assistant does. Then add the conflict rule.

    Conflict rule to add
    # Add to the rules once you have seen the conflict handled badly
5. If two documents disagree, name both sources and say that they differ. Do not pick one.
   Then point the person to HR for the final answer.
   Example: "The handbook [handbook.pdf §3.2] says 20 days and the leave policy
   [leave-policy.pdf §2.1] says 22. These differ. Please confirm with HR."

    Notice: before the rule, most assistants quietly pick one number. After it, the answer shows both. That silent pick is the most dangerous failure a policy assistant can have, because it looks exactly like a right answer.

  6. Ask the assistant for one Artifact: "Make a one-page New starter FAQ as an Artifact: the ten questions a new starter is most likely to ask in their first month, each answered in two lines with the document and section." Then ask for one change and check the version history.

    Notice: the FAQ is a thing you could hand to a real new starter, with the sources attached. The chat is where you made it; the Artifact is what you keep.

Check yourself

Eight quick questions

Pick an answer to see why it is right or wrong. Score 80 percent or more to pass. Nobody is watching; the point is to find out what did not stick.

Think it through

Why does a Project help with the "close the chat and it forgets" problem from Week 1?

In Week 1 the chat's only memory was its context window, and closing the chat emptied it. A Project keeps the files and the instructions outside any single chat and loads them into every new one. The memory now lives in the Project, not in the conversation, so nothing is lost when a chat ends. What a Project does not do is remember the chats themselves: chat 2 knows the binder and the rules, not what chat 1 decided.

What happens if you upload 300 pages of documents to a Project?

At roughly 500 tokens a page, 300 pages is about 150,000 tokens. If Claude can still fit that in the window it will read it whole into every chat, leaving little room for the conversation and asking the model to find one clause in a very long context. Past the point where it no longer fits, Claude switches to retrieval and pulls only the best-matching sections for each question, which works well when the documents have clear titles and numbered sections and badly when they are scans without headings. Either way, the better move is usually to split the knowledge into focused Projects. Week 5 builds the retrieval machinery by hand.

Why is "only answer from the files" a critical rule for a policy assistant and a bad rule for a brainstorming assistant?

A policy assistant must be correct and traceable. An invented leave rule can cost a real person money or a job, so a refusal is better than a guess, and a citation is better than either. A brainstorming assistant has the opposite job: you want ideas beyond what is already written down. The same rule that protects staff would make it refuse the whole task. The rule follows from the job, not from the technology.

A colleague wants to upload last year's salary spreadsheet to the shared policy Project so the assistant can answer pay questions. What do you say?

No, and the reason is structural rather than cautious: everything in a Project's knowledge is readable by everyone in the Project, so a salary file in a shared Project is a salary file published to the company. Pay questions are also personal, not policy, and the people who asked for the policy helper did not consent to that. If pay questions matter, they need a different design: a separate Project restricted to the payroll team, or, later in the course, a tool with access control and a person approving each answer. This is exactly what the "never upload" line in design-log entry 3 is for.

Practice

Should it answer?

Eight staff questions reach your policy helper. For each one, read what the documents contain, then pick what a well-instructed assistant should do. Answer with a citation, say it is not covered, or hand over to HR or a manager.
